chunks: Rijal al-Kashi: Hamduwayh, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhayna, from Zurara who said:

I was seated in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) together with Humran, when Humran said to him: What do you say about what Zurara says, for I have opposed him in it? He (Abu Abdillah) said: And what is that? He (Humran) said: He (Zurara) believes that the timings of the prayers were delegated to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and that he was the one who fixed them. He (Abu Abdillah) said: And what do you say? I said: Verily Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him on the first day with the first time and on the second day with the last time, then Jibril said: O Muhammad, what is between them is the time. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: O Humran, verily what Zurara means is that Jibril came to indicate to Muhammad (peace be upon him). Zurara has spoken the truth, for that was given to Muhammad (peace be upon him) and he fixed it, and Jibril (peace be upon him) gave only indications about it.
ai.seo_question: How were the specific times for daily prayers determined according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kashi highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between divine indication (ishara) and legislative authority (fawd), affirming that while Jibril signaled the temporal boundaries, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) possessed the delegated authority to establish the precise prayer times. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) reconciles the views of Zurara and Humran by validating the Prophet's active role in defining the intervals, thereby emphasizing the concept of 'fawd' (delegation) in Islamic jurisprudence. This underscores the Prophet's dual role as both recipient of revelation and active legislator within the framework of divine will.
